title: Mastery Challenge: Psychology
objective: After this level you can demonstrate command of Psychology Levels 1 to 99 across the whole tree.
summary: Questions from across the tree: how psychology studies the mind, what counts as a disorder, how therapy is tested, and why good science keeps checking itself. Every question can be corrected.

cards.headline: The Psychology Mastery Challenge.
cards.body: Questions from across the tree, from the first psychology lab to the replication crisis. Level 1 asked how you study a mind nobody can see. Now show how far you've come. Take your time: every question can be corrected.

cards.headline: Psychology: mastered
learned: How psychology turns questions about an unseen mind into ideas it can test, and keeps what survives.
What separates a mental disorder from an ordinary struggle, and why diagnosis belongs to professionals.
Why famous findings like power posing faded, and how psychologists now guard against false results.
How to talk about mental health without stigma, and where to point someone who needs help.

questions.prompt: What made Wundt's 1879 Leipzig lab the start of psychology as a science?

options.label: He brought experiments to questions philosophy had only argued over
He was the first to treat patients with talk therapy
options.rationale: Talk therapy was Freud's psychoanalysis.

options.label: He showed the mind works like a computer
options.rationale: That picture came with the cognitive revolution, decades later.

options.label: He studied only behavior anyone could observe
options.rationale: That was Watson's behaviorism.

questions.explanation: Wundt set up the first psychology lab in 1879 and insisted on experiments borrowed from the natural sciences.

questions.prompt: Behaviorism set the mind aside. What revived scientific interest in the mind by the 1950s?

options.label: Freud's idea of an unconscious mind
options.rationale: Freud's ideas came long before and weren't what revived it.

options.label: Wundt's reaction-time experiments in Leipzig
options.rationale: Wundt's lab opened in 1879, before behaviorism.

options.label: New work in linguistics, neuroscience and computers
Twin studies of genes and environment
options.rationale: Those study genes and environment, not the return of the mind.

questions.explanation: New work in linguistics, neuroscience and computer science brought the mind back: the cognitive revolution.

questions.prompt: Which of these runs in families yet has a heritability of zero?

options.label: Hair color
options.rationale: Hair color is highly heritable, even though dye changes it.

options.label: The language you speak
Every trait that twins share
options.rationale: Heritability varies from trait to trait.

options.label: Nothing; anything that runs in families is genetic
options.rationale: Language runs in families without being genetic.

questions.explanation: Language runs in families but isn't under genetic control, so its heritability is zero.

questions.prompt: Which 1979 document set out respect for persons, beneficence and justice for research on people?

options.label: The Nuremberg Code
options.rationale: That came in 1947, after the Nazi doctors' trial.

options.label: The National Research Act
options.rationale: That 1974 law created the commission that wrote it.

options.label: The DSM-5-TR
options.rationale: That's a diagnostic manual from 2022.

options.label: The Belmont Report

questions.explanation: The Belmont Report of 1979 set out respect for persons, beneficence and justice.

questions.prompt: Red hair is uncommon. Why isn't it a mental disorder?

options.label: It causes no significant disturbance, distress or impairment
Because it runs in families, so it's genetic
options.rationale: Many conditions run in families; heritability isn't the test.

options.label: Because the DSM only lists common traits
options.rationale: Being common or rare isn't what the DSM looks at.

options.label: Because only rare traits can count as disorders
options.rationale: Rarity alone is never enough.

questions.explanation: Being atypical isn't enough: a disorder is a clinically significant disturbance, usually with distress or problems functioning.

questions.prompt: Which statement about depression fits the current evidence?

options.label: Depression is simply low serotonin
options.rationale: A 2022 review found no consistent evidence for that.

options.label: The one-chemical story is too simple, yet antidepressants help many
Since serotonin isn't the cause, antidepressants can't work
options.rationale: A 2018 analysis of 522 trials found they beat placebo.

options.label: Depression has one cause: stressful events
options.rationale: Genes, biology and psychology play roles too.

questions.explanation: Several factors combine in depression; the chemical-imbalance story is too simple, but antidepressants still help many people.

questions.prompt: What does cognitive behavioral therapy mainly work on?

options.label: Hidden childhood memories reached through dreams
options.rationale: That's closer to Freud's psychoanalysis.

options.label: Medication doses only
options.rationale: CBT is a talking therapy.

options.label: Current problems and how thoughts, feelings and actions link
Reaction times measured to a thousandth of a second
options.rationale: That was Wundt's lab.

questions.explanation: CBT treats thoughts, feelings, sensations and actions as linked and focuses on current problems.

options.label: "A schizophrenic"
options.rationale: That defines someone by a diagnosis.

options.label: "That's so crazy"
options.rationale: Casual "crazy" feeds stereotypes.

options.label: "Committed suicide"
options.rationale: NIMH advises avoiding this wording.

options.label: "A person with schizophrenia"

questions.explanation: Person-first language puts the person before the diagnosis: "a person with schizophrenia".

questions.prompt: The "When I'm Sixty-Four" demonstration and Carney's account of her self-report measure share which lesson?

options.label: Hormone tests can never be trusted in psychology
options.rationale: Neither case is about hormone tests.

options.label: Choosing measures after seeing results can fake an effect
Large samples are what create false findings
options.rationale: Small samples and flexible choices are the problem.

options.label: A popular talk is enough to confirm a finding
options.rationale: Popularity isn't evidence.

questions.explanation: Both show that choosing, after the fact, which measures to report can make a weak or impossible effect look real.

questions.prompt: From Level 1's publishing rule to the 2015 replication project: what makes a psychology finding trustworthy?

options.label: One striking result in a top journal
options.rationale: Many such results failed on a rerun.

options.label: A famous talk that millions have watched
options.rationale: Power posing had that, and still faded.

options.label: How confident the original author is
options.rationale: Confidence isn't evidence.

options.label: Other researchers repeat it and find it again

questions.explanation: Psychologists publish so others can repeat their work; findings that replicate earn trust, and many famous ones didn't.
